questions.question: 1. Grain boundary has a dimension of:

explanations.a: Incorrect – Grain boundaries are not point defects; they extend over a region between grains rather than being localized points.
explanations.b: Incorrect – A grain boundary is not a one-dimensional line; it separates grains over an area in a material.
explanations.c: Correct – Grain boundaries are two-dimensional defects because they form interfaces (surfaces) between adjacent crystals or grains.
explanations.d: Incorrect – Grain boundaries do not occupy a volume like bulk phases; they are interfacial (surface) defects.

explanations.a: Correct – Fine grain size generally increases strength (Hall–Petch relationship) and also improves toughness by hindering crack propagation and allowing more uniform deformation.
explanations.b: Incorrect – While fine grains increase strength, they do not reduce toughness; toughness usually improves or is maintained rather than becoming low.
explanations.c: Incorrect – Fine grain size does not reduce strength; instead, smaller grains increase grain boundary area which strengthens the material.
explanations.d: Incorrect – Fine grains do not lead to both low strength and low toughness; this contradicts the Hall–Petch effect.

answers.a: fine grain promote crack initiation, whereas coarse grain resist crack propagation
answers.b: fine grain promote crack initiation, and coarse grain promote crack propagation
answers.c: fine grain resist crack initiation, and coarse grain resist crack propagation
answers.d: fine grain resist crack initiation, whereas coarse grain promote crack propagation

explanations.a: Incorrect – Fine grains do not promote crack initiation; instead, they generally help resist crack initiation. Also, coarse grains are not inherently better at resisting crack propagation.
explanations.b: Incorrect – Fine grains do not promote crack initiation, and coarse grains do not specifically promote crack propagation in fatigue behavior.
explanations.c: Incorrect – Coarse grains do not typically resist crack propagation better; fine grains are more effective in hindering both initiation and early propagation.
explanations.d: Correct – Fine grains resist crack initiation due to more grain boundaries acting as barriers, while coarse grains tend to allow easier crack propagation, reducing fatigue resistance.

questions.question: 4. Pearlite structure of steel has which type of grains:

explanations.a: Incorrect – Equiaxed grains are roughly equal in all dimensions and are typical of many cast or recrystallized structures, but not specific to pearlite.
explanations.b: Incorrect – Columnar grains are elongated grains formed during directional solidification, not characteristic of pearlite.
explanations.c: Correct – Pearlite has a lamellar structure consisting of alternating layers (lamellae) of ferrite and cementite, giving it a layered appearance.
explanations.d: Incorrect – Dendritic grains are tree-like solidification structures seen in casting, not in pearlite microstructure.

questions.question: 5. Cast structure showing constitutional supercooling typically will result which grain-structure:

explanations.a: Incorrect – Equiaxed grains form under high nucleation conditions and relatively uniform cooling, not specifically due to constitutional supercooling.
explanations.b: Incorrect – Columnar grains form when there is a strong directional temperature gradient and limited nucleation, not due to constitutional supercooling.
explanations.c: Incorrect – Lamellar structure is characteristic of pearlite in steel, not related to cast solidification under constitutional supercooling.
explanations.d: Correct – Constitutional supercooling leads to instability of the solid–liquid interface, promoting dendritic growth during solidification in cast structures.

questions.question: 6. Martensitic grain structure is typically exhibits which grain structure?

explanations.a: Incorrect – Equiaxed grains are common in recrystallized or cast structures, not in martensite, which forms through a diffusionless transformation.
explanations.b: Incorrect – Columnar grains are associated with directional solidification, not martensitic transformation in steels.
explanations.c: Incorrect – Bimodal grains refer to a mixture of two distinct grain sizes, which is not characteristic of martensitic structure.
explanations.d: Correct – Martensitic steel typically exhibits lath-type (or plate-like) grain/sub-grain structures formed by rapid, diffusionless transformation of austenite.
